The proposal would have transformed a cattle property into one of Australia's biggest fruit farms, growing mandarins, grapes, avocados, and melons. But the traditional owners argued that water and water-access sites hold deep cultural significance in these arid lands, and that the 30-year licence threatened sacred sites and the native plants and animals dependent on the aquifer. After losing their case in lower courts over four years, the native title holders prevailed when the High Court found the responsible minister had failed to properly justify the extended licence term and had not given the corporation a fair opportunity to argue about the conditions attached to the permit.
The case highlights a question that reaches beyond one water licence: how development decisions in Australia balance economic ambitions with cultural rights and environmental stewardship, especially in regions where water is both scarce and sacred. The licence will now be quashed and sent back for reconsideration, offering traditional owners a seat at the table in decisions about resources that have sustained their culture for generations.

item.title: Injured Capybara Flees Fire and Is Rescued in Saquarema EPA; Opossum with 7 Babies Also Among Animals Saved
item.description:
Environmental guards in Saquarema, Brazil, have been rescuing wildlife from a two-day fire consuming the Massambaba Environmental Protection Area. Among those saved was a capybara—the world's largest rodent—fleeing the flames with visible burns. The injured animal was taken to veterinary care, while rescue teams also found an opossum with seven babies, a boa constrictor, and a hedgehog, all released safely in protected areas once checked.
The fire spread through vegetation including cattails, wetland plants that typically grow along rivers and marshes, signaling how deeply the blaze penetrated the ecosystem. Firefighting efforts required aircraft support, complicated by the fact that local hydrants were dry due to scheduled maintenance. The water company stated the outage had been communicated in advance, though they hadn't been notified of the fire and maintained tanker trucks for emergency support. Over 95% of forest fires in the region have human causes, whether accidental or intentional.
While Saquarema has seen fewer vegetation fires this year compared to last—86 versus 177 in the same period—these blazes continue destroying protected habitats, threatening wildlife, and creating health risks from smoke. The story quietly underscores an ongoing tension between human activity and fragile ecosystems, where even routine maintenance can compound natural disasters, and where the smallest spark can send creatures fleeing for their lives across charred ground.

item.title: Court reduces nursing technician's work hours without salary cut to care for father with cancer in ES
item.description:
A Brazilian labor court has upheld a remarkable decision allowing a nursing technician in Espírito Santo to halve his working hours—from 36 to 18 hours per week—without any reduction in salary or requirement to make up the time. The reason: his 75-year-old father requires full-time care after being diagnosed with multiple myeloma, an incurable blood cancer, along with chronic kidney disease, diabetes, hypertension, and stroke complications. As an only child, the technician presented medical documentation proving his father needs constant assistance with daily activities and medical appointments.
The case raised a legal question, as Brazil's standard labor code doesn't explicitly provide for such arrangements. The employer, a public company, argued the technician didn't meet criteria for special scheduling and noted he holds another public position with a 40-hour workweek. However, Judge Xeres Gusmão applied an analogous interpretation, borrowing from public servant regulations to protect what he considered fundamental rights: human dignity, family bonds, and health. The appeals panel agreed, with Judge Valério Soares Heringer emphasizing that the father's clinical condition justified the flexibility, given the worker's "indisputable need to stay close to his elderly parent, afflicted by serious illness and completely dependent." The court also confirmed the technician's right to receive a disability assistance benefit for dependents, as outlined in collective labor agreements.
This decision quietly highlights how legal systems can stretch to accommodate caregiving realities that formal codes haven't yet addressed. It's a story worth attention not for drama, but for its gentle insistence that work structures can bend when family need becomes urgent—a recognition that sometimes the most important labor happens outside the workplace.

item.title: Family, friends and fans celebrate Johan Lomu's untold story at emotional NZ documentary premiere
item.description:
A new documentary about rugby legend Jonah Lomu brought hundreds of family, friends, and fans to tears at its New Zealand premiere in Auckland. The film offers an intimate portrait of the All Black icon through never-before-seen home videos and perspectives from those who knew him best, revealing the man behind the global sports phenomenon.
The Lomu family had long dreamed of sharing Jonah's story on their own terms. Aging VHS tapes sat in storage, holding precious memories that risked being lost to time. The documentary provided an opportunity not only to preserve this footage digitally but to present Jonah's life through a Pacific cultural lens. His younger brother John emphasized that the story "was never ours to keep, but also share with everybody else." Attendees praised the film's respectful, heartfelt approach, with one saying it was "nice to see our people being preserved in a really good way." Former teammate Kevin Mealamu, who once played Lomu on PlayStation before playing alongside him as an All Black, hopes the film will inspire younger generations the way Jonah inspired him.
This documentary is a quiet act of cultural preservation and generational bridge-building. It captures not just athletic greatness but the values of faith, hard work, and perseverance that defined Lomu's journey. For Pacific communities and rugby fans worldwide, it's a chance to meet the person beyond the legend and to carry forward a legacy that reminds us, as John Lomu puts it, that dreams are possible when you "just go out and go for it."

item.title: VIDEO: Right whale and calf 'dance' in photographer's footage at Arpoador
item.description:
A photographer in Rio de Janeiro captured a rare and tender moment: a southern right whale and her calf appearing to "dance" together in the waters off Arpoador beach. The footage shows the calf climbing onto its mother's back, a behavior that looks playful but serves a vital purpose—the young whale is resting and seeking protection. As photographer Gabriel Klabin noted, "It looks like play, but it's survival."
The southern right whale is classified as endangered in Brazil, still recovering from the devastating impact of commercial whaling. While these whales migrate regularly to Brazilian waters during winter and spring for breeding, they typically concentrate along the coast of Santa Catarina. Sightings near Rio de Janeiro are uncommon, making this encounter particularly special. The article also touches on the more frequent presence of humpback whales in the region, which travel up to 9,000 kilometers from Antarctica to the warmer waters of Bahia's Abrolhos Archipelago to mate and give birth, with Rio serving as a waypoint along their remarkable journey.
This story offers a quiet reminder of nature's resilience and the ongoing recovery of species once pushed to the brink. The increasing whale sightings along Brazil's coast reflect decades of conservation efforts following the ban on commercial whaling in the 1980s. What makes this moment meaningful is its rarity—a glimpse of maternal care in an endangered species, captured in an urban setting where ocean and city meet.
